note: Ben fell off the climbing frame and cried. Told the director.
why: Plain injury note. A control: the rules should already catch it.

note: Omar got a nosebleed during circle time and we sent him to the nurse.
why: An injury written as one compound word.

note: Zara said her dad hits her when he is angry.
why: A safeguarding disclosure. It must never be turned into a skill suggestion.

note: Noah threw up after lunch and said his tummy felt funny.
why: An illness written in everyday words.

note: Maya fell asleep during story time, so we let her rest.
why: Uses the word 'fell' but nothing is wrong. A false alarm sends a harmless note to an incident record.

note: Sam hit the drum in time with the song and kept the beat.
Jay loved the fall leaves and sorted them by colour.
why: 'Fall' is a season here. The sorting is real learning evidence that a false alarm would hide.

note: Leo did not count the blocks. He knocked them over and laughed.
why: The child did not count. A suggestion for counting would be wrong.

note: Ria wouldn't use the scissors, so we tried tearing paper instead.
why: The child refused the scissors. A fine-motor suggestion would be wrong.

note: Noah didn't give up on the puzzle and tried again by himself.
why: A guard against over-fixing: this negation is positive evidence of persistence and must still match.

note: Ria held her crayon with a tripod grasp.
why: A teacher says 'grasp' where the rules only know 'grip'.

note: Leo built a really big tall tower out of blocks.
Leo counted the blocks, built a tall tower and shared his blocks with Maya.
why: A control: three skills match, never more than two are suggested, both children are found.

note: Everyone was a bit loud this morning after the rain.
why: A control: 'a bit loud' is not a bite, and nothing here is a learning moment.
